title: Testing React Components with Testing Library

subChunks.title: Testing React Components with Testing Library
subChunks.hookHtml: Component tests verify that your UI works correctly for the user — not that your implementation details work correctly for the developer. React Testing Library's core philosophy: test what the user sees and does, not what your component's internal state is. This philosophy leads to tests that survive refactors and catch real regressions.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The testing philosophy

The more your tests resemble the way your software is used, the more confidence they can give you. — Kent C. Dodds

Testing Library queries elements the way users find them: by text, by label, by role. Not by CSS class, not by component name, not by internal state.

Setup and basic rendering

import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react';
import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';
import Counter from './Counter';

test('renders initial count', () => {
  render(<Counter />);
  expect(screen.getByText('Count: 0')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Querying elements

// By text (partial match with regex):
screen.getByText(/count: 0/i);

// By accessible role:
screen.getByRole('button', { name: /increment/i });
screen.getByRole('heading', { name: /quest log/i });

// By label (form inputs):
screen.getByLabelText(/email/i);

// By test id (last resort — use when no semantic alternative exists):
screen.getByTestId('submit-button');

// Checking existence without throwing:
screen.queryByText('Error') // returns null if not found
screen.findByText('Loaded!') // async — waits for element to appear

Simulating user interaction

import userEvent from '@testing-library/user-event';

test('increments count when button clicked', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<Counter />);

  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /increment/i }));

  expect(screen.getByText('Count: 1')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

test('typing into an input updates displayed value', async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<SearchBox />);

  await user.type(screen.getByLabelText(/search/i), 'frost mage');

  expect(screen.getByDisplayValue('frost mage')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Testing async behaviour

test('shows data after fetch', async () => {
  // Mock the fetch:
  global.fetch = jest.fn().mockResolvedValue({
    ok: true,
    json: async () => ({ name: 'Aria' }),
  });

  render(<UserProfile userId={1} />);

  // Wait for async update:
  expect(await screen.findByText('Aria')).toBeInTheDocument();
});

Vex: "getBy throws if the element isn't found — use for things that must exist. queryBy returns null — use for asserting something does NOT exist. findBy is async — use for things that appear after a delay. Know the three families and you know the query API."

What not to test

  • Internal state values — test the visible output they produce
  • Component method names — test what they do, not what they're called
  • CSS classes applied for purely visual reasons
  • Implementation details that can change without affecting user experience

storyBeats.text: Vex sits across from a user — not a developer. 'I don't care what's inside the component,' the user says. 'I care if clicking the button makes the number go up.' Vex nods. 'Then that's what we test.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: The test should be written from the user's perspective. The user sees text, clicks buttons, fills in forms. The test should do the same. If you find yourself asserting state values or checking CSS classes — stop. Ask: what does the user see when this works correctly?

storyBeats.speaker: User-centric test

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write tests for a <Counter /> component (provided in starter code). Your test file should verify:

  • It renders with count 0
  • Clicking 'Increment' increases the count to 1
  • Clicking 'Increment' twice increases to 2
  • Clicking 'Reset' returns count to 0

Use @testing-library/react and @testing-library/user-event.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Write a test suite for the LoginForm from rx-jun-4 (or build a simple one to test). Cover: renders email and password fields, shows validation errors on empty submit, calls onSubmit with correct data on valid submit, disables submit button while submitting. Use mocks for the async onSubmit prop.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between getBy, queryBy, and findBy queries in Testing Library. Give a concrete use case for each. Then explain why Testing Library discourages testing internal state — what does it encourage you to test instead?

questions.prompt: What is the difference between `screen.getByText` and `screen.queryByText`?
options: getByText throws if the element is not found; queryByText returns null
queryByText is async; getByText is synchronous
getByText matches exact text; queryByText matches partial text
They are identical — queryBy is an alias for getBy
questions.answer: getByText throws if the element is not found; queryByText returns null
questions.explanation: getBy* queries are for elements that must exist — they throw immediately if not found, giving a clear error. queryBy* queries are for asserting absence — they return null instead of throwing, so you can write: expect(screen.queryByText('Error')).not.toBeInTheDocument().

questions.prompt: A component fetches data and shows a loading state, then the user's name. How do you test that the name appears?
questions.explanation: findBy* queries are async — they poll until the element appears or a timeout is exceeded. They return a Promise, so you await them. This is the correct pattern for asserting elements that appear asynchronously after data loads.

questions.prompt: Why does Testing Library recommend querying by role over querying by test ID?
options: Role queries test accessibility — they verify the element is semantically correct and discoverable by assistive technology
Role queries are faster to write
Test IDs require adding data attributes to every element
Role queries survive component refactors better because roles don't change
questions.answer: Role queries test accessibility — they verify the element is semantically correct and discoverable by assistive technology
questions.explanation: getByRole('button', { name: /submit/ }) asserts that there's a properly labelled button — which means screen readers can find it too. It tests both functionality and accessibility. data-testid is a valid fallback when no semantic alternative exists, but it's a last resort — it tests nothing about the element's semantic meaning.
